The Rocket Files BY JODY DUNCAN roasting significantly different backstories and superpowers, all of the Marvel superheroes enjoying cinematic treatment to date have had one thing in common: All have performed their super-heroics principally on Planet Earth. Guardians of the Galaxy, Marvel Studios' most recent release, directed by James Gunn, breaks that mold with a story that sets a band of intergalactic misfits against villains whose imperial aspirations are cosmic rather than global in scale. The film starts with the alien abduction of an apparently fatherless young boy, Peter Quill (Wyatt Oleff), whose mother has just died. The story then jumps 26 years into the future. A grown Peter (Chris Pratt) - also known as Star-Lord - has become a cocky, irreverent and somewhat reckless 'ravager' who engages in interplanetary theft under the auspices of his abductor, Yondu (Michael Rooker). When Quill comes into possession of an orb housing a Power Stone capable of destroying entire galaxies, he makes a wary alliance with the green-skinned, rebellious Gamora (Zoe Saldana), Rocket, a genetically engineered raccoon (voiced by Bradley Cooper), the powerfully built and tattooed Drax 1 / 27 the Destroyer (Dave Bautista), and the tree-like humanoid Groot (voiced by Vin Diesel) to

GUARDIANS keep the orb out of the hands of those who would use it for nefarious ends. With both Rocket and Groot realized entirely via computer animation, and with scenes set in many exotic cosmic worlds, Guardians of the Galaxy relied heavily on visual effects, supervised on the production side by Stephane Ceretti. The majority of the film's 2,000-plus visual effects shots were awarded to Framestore and MPC, with Proof, Luma Pictures, Method Studios, Cantina Creative, Lola VFA, The Third Floor and Sony Pictures Imageworks lending critical support. Preproduction started in January 2012, with James Gunn and key personnel working at Marvel's Manhattan Studios offices. "James was preparing as much as he could," said Stephane Ceretti, ¿doing thumbnails and his own storyboards. We also started prevising with previs supervisor Earl Hibbert and his team from Proof, which immediately started doing environments and building assets. Then we all moved to London, where we prevised pretty much the entire movie. In addition to blocking out action, Gunn worked out many of the movie's physical gags in previs. "Adding humor to the action sequences was very important to James," said Earl Hibbert,and we worked with him on that quite extensively in the previs process. All of the humor and gags James wanted were right there in the previs, and when he showed it to execs, they would laugh - and that's how we knew we had it right. If a gag worked in the previs phase, with our low-res animated characters, it would be even funnier when the actors were doing it. By the end of the process, Proof had generated a full hour and 15 minutes of previs representing nearly every scene in the final movie. 2 / 27 Preproduction also saw the initiation of tests for the film's two principal animated

GUARDIANS characters - Rocket and Groot. "We wanted to figure out the best way of approaching these characters," said Stephane Ceretti, "so we came up with the idea of doing a short movie about how Rocket and Groot met. We shot some plates in London for that test, and then gave those to several effects studios to build and animate the characters, working with Rocket and Groot designs that had come out of the Marvel art department. All of the vendors came up with some pretty good animation pieces that illustrated how Rocket and Groot would work together with their respective sizes, how we might frame them together in shots, et cetera. Of course, we had preconceived ideas about all of that, but it was good to try out those ideas before we started to shoot. Shepperton and Longcross Studios housed the production, which was characterized by large-scale sets and special effects gags, and hundreds of practical makeups to represent the various alien species populating the galaxy. Special makeup effects supervisor David White and his team created the practical makeups for lead characters such as Gamora, Drax, Yondu, Ronan (Lee Pace), Korath (Djimon Hounsou) and Nebula (Karen Gillan), as well as for dozens of supporting and background alien characters. Despite his human rather than alien physiology, Drax was among the most difficult of the practical makeup effects, due to the tattoos that covered him from head to toe.iThe first Drax makeup test took seven or eight hours to apply," recalled Ceretti, "which was just not practical. Then they came up with the idea of painting just his head, and having him wear a T-shirt that had the tattoos painted on it, and melding that T-shirt with his body — and that worked pretty well. There were wrinkles that formed in the T-shirt when 3 / 27 he moved, though, which required a lot of post work by Lola. They had to smooth out the

wrinkles on this moving character, while retaining the shape and texture of the tattoos." effects for the sequence, developing the rocky Morag environment and extending a small stage set. MPC started with reference photography of the Grand Canyon, as well as the White Desert in Egypt, shapes from which were replicated on the backlot set at Longcross. "We ended up going with a more graphic and dramatic look for Morag," said MPC visual effects supervisor Nicolas Aithadi. It's one of my favorite environments because it has a texture to it that is really nice. Our environment lead, Marco Rolandi, did a great job with the Morag environment." The story then moves to Xandar, capital of the Nova Empire, where the future Guardians are first brought together. Gunn shot live-action Xandar scenes, including an extended fight as Gamora and Quill wrestle for possession of the orb, on partial sets built by production designer Charles Wood and his team at Longcross Studios. Partial sets representing the mall site of the fight consisted of half a round-shaped shop, a walkway with glass railings, and a pond. "The Xandar mall was supposed to be two levels," said Stephane Ceretti, "but we built only one. So we shot what was supposed to be the upper level, and then we redressed that as the lower level, and shot on that. Then MPC extended it, building all of Xandar as a synthetic city." Marco Rolandi and CG supervisor Daniele Bigi led the build of Xandar at MPC.iWe GUARDIANS fter the pre-credits sequence with Peter Quill as a young boy, the film jumps to the surface of the planet Morag where the grown Peter finds the filigreed silver orb. GUARDIANS not only had to build the entire city to accommodate all of the sequences set in Xandar," said Nicolas Aithadi, iwe had to build it at different altitudes - everything from 30,000 feet high to ground leveli MPC started with concept art from Marvel, including what the team called 'the Google map,' which was a top-down view of the city illustrating its overall shape and layout, but consisting only of simple cubes to represent buildings. 'The city's shape was actually the Nova Corps logo, so it was quite specific," noted Aithadi. "But, otherwise, they let us come up with the final look of the city, translating the cubes into actual structures. We tried to create architectures and shapes that would feel extraterrestrial. We looked at some interesting real-world architecture, structures in Shanghai and Dubai that had an alien look to them, and then Marco and his team transformed those buildings into architecture that was specific to Xandar. Once we'd come up with some basic shapes and styles for buildings, we tried to create a sense of history in the city, with some areas having buildings that looked like they'd been there for 300 years, and others with buildings that were all shiny and newii In addition to buildings, the synthetic city was comprised of gardens and tens of thousands of trees. "We added parks and paths around the buildings," recounted Daniele Bigi, ichanging the types of trees based on the terrain formation. We left the vegetation growing in a more organic way in the suburbs and peripheral areas, and generated more perfectly designed gardens close to the city center. A bigger percentage of flowers and colorful plants was added close to beautiful beaches. We also designed marinas and 5 / 27 specific Xandar yachts. Since Xandar is a city on an island, developing the water sur-

GUARDIANS rounding it was another key element. In order to get the correct tropical feeling we had to start from the seabed. We looked at digital elevation maps as reference, and scattered texture maps with corals, rocks and different types of sand, which gave us the correct refracted colors once we put the water layer on top. Our environment lead, Alexandru Popescu, played a fundamental role in transforming all of these ideas into CG reality." he full CG city represented a very large amount of data and was rendered at varcity," said Nicolas Aithadi, "which was level of detail C - the lower-resolution city as we would see it from the sky. We built that one first, just so we could define the entire layout. For shots on the ground, such as those in the mall fight, we had the higher-rez version, which had windows in buildings, floors, walls and pillars. We dressed all of the buildings with chairs, tables - everything we could think of to make it look detailed and complex, to compensate for the fact that there wasn't much there in the plates, in terms of set. For the immediate backdrop of the mall, MPC built a large CG building from photographs and scans of the Liège Train Station in Belgium. It is on the Xandar mall that Quill first comes into contact with Rocket and his sidekick, Groot. James Gunn's brother, Sean, played Rocket on set, while a mime stood in for Groot. Both performers - wearing green- or blue-colored suits to facilitate their removal from plates - guided eyelines and camera framing, and gave the other actors something with which to interact. 6 / 27 Early in production, visual effects experimented with doing motion capture on the

GUARDIANS Groot performer, for animation purposes. "We wanted to do some animation studies with a real person doing what Groot would do," said Stephane Ceretti. "But in the end, after talking to the vendors and to James, we decided not to use motion capture on set. It would have interrupted the flow, and would have slowed things down - and James likes to shoot fast. So we decided to go for full keyframe animation for both Rocket and Groot." The nearly seven-foot-tall mime was approximately the right height for Groot, especially after donning a helmet and mask. The performer in the helmet allowed the actors to look at Groot at the right height," explained Ceretti. "We also had a little person that was about the size of Rocket, and we used her for camera line-ups. The camera crew could line up everybody, knowing everyone's placement, and then we would go into a proper line-up with the actors, and with Sean Gunn either squatting or on his knees, talking to the actors and performing as Rocket. That was our master shot for performance. And then we would take everybody out, put in some tennis balls on sticks or laser pointers to keep the eyelines correct, and the actors would play the scene without Rocket or Groot - although Sean would still be there, off-camera, delivering Rocket's lines. Sean Gunn captured the spirit of Rocket's character from the get-go. "I think James actually had his brother in mind when he was writing Rocket,i related Framestore visual effects supervisor Jonathan Fawkner. So they placed Sean into the shots to deliver all the lines that Rocket had, even for closeupsi Framestore took the lead in building the CG Rocket, and shared that asset with MPC for its many shots featuring the character. Likewise, MPC took the lead in developing 7 / 27 Groot, and shared that model with Framestore. "Rather than share shots," noted Fawk-

ner, we shared assets. One of the reasons we had to split the show so unconventionally was that Rocket and Groot were essentially in every shot, and they were in every shot together. So we shared models, and even shared caches of fur. But it was a very hard thing to match these assets up. I think we got the easier end of the bargain, because although Groot was very difficult to rig, and it took MPC just as long to prep Groot as it took us to prep Rocket, matching the look of a furry creature is a much harder thing to do." noon studying Oreo, petting him and photographing him extensively. 'James would go through every shot with us and explain what the point of the shot was and what he wanted Rocket to convey. And he never deviated from that. Only in the final stages of animation did the animators incorporate raccoon behaviors into Rocket's performance. James wanted an actor more than he wanted a raccoon," noted Fawkner. "We had done some early animation studies with more raccoon behaviors, but Marvel and James never responded well to those tests. Later on, though, we started introducing the odd nose twitch and ear scratch. The one character trait James did emphasize was that he wanted Rocket to be very nimble with his hands. He often said, 'If Rocket has a super-power, it is his super hands.' And so we found moments in our sequences to highlight Rocket's hand movements. Overall, though, James was happy with Rocket not doing too much, and he often had to restrain our animators' ambition. If you're an animator and you've got a shot that's a second long, you try to make that shot sing from start to finish. But James wasn't looking for that. He was much more concerned with the sequence as a whole, rather than with every detail of one character's performance. That restraint was evident in Rocket's lip sync, as well, as Gunn often asked animators to reduce the character's mouth movements. "From the start," recalled Fawkner, "James said that he thought animated animals often looked like they were over articu9 / 27 lating, as if the animators had worked extra hard to create the mouth shapes. He said:

'That's when they stop looking real. It looks amazing, but it's too much.' So we were restrained in the mouth movements for Rocket. The interesting thing, though, is that Bradley Cooper has a large mouth, and he articulates a lot when delivering lines. So we were trying to match Bradley, but more often than not, an exact match was too much movement for James." goes along the length," explained Fawkner. "Sometimes the colors are short, and sometimes they re long - and the nature of that combination really affected the overall color of his fur." Complicating the issue further, the company was rendering in Solid Angle's Arnold, which meant every aspect of the character had to be set up for ray-tracing. That gave us some areas for concern because we had a furry creature in which every hair had to shadow every other hair. At the best of times, our enemy is noise. Can we get our renders through fast enough without a lot of noise? Most of the hard work in look-dev and coding goes into trying to reduce that problem. Ultimately, we ran up against quite long render times - but that was just the nature of the beast. Rocket ended up being an incredibly robust asset. By the time we had finished dev-ing him, we could stick him in low light inside a space pod, or put him outside and in bright daylight. We put him into the middle of various battles with flashes and fire. Wherever we put him, his fur scattered beautifully. GUARDIANS MPC adapted the Rocket asset to its pipeline and incorporated the character into its Xandar sequence, which also featured Groot - the character for which MPC took the lead. Just as Framestore had with Rocket, MPC artists started with Marvel concept renderings of Groot. "We received loads of concepts of Groot," recalled Nicolas Aithadi, "but they were quite different from the Groot we ended up with. The original versions were very tree-like, which made it more difficult to relate to him. So we humanized him a bit, making his face more appealing and relatable. James wanted people to fall in love with Groot, and to see him as this very gentle and kind character. At the same time, Groot could be very fierce and aggressive. We had to find both Groots and make them live together in the same character. We spent a good six or seven months developing Groot, from the broad strokes to the fine details." Though he appears as a rather simple character - a trunk with branches - Groot required some extremely complex modeling, rigging and animation from rigging lead Ben Jones, animation supervisor Greg Fisher and their crews. One of the early animation decisions for Groot was to keep him more or less rigid, without a lot of deformations that would have created a kind of 'Gumby' look. It didn't make sense for a character made of wood to bend too much," noted Aithadi. "We didn't want an elastic body. So we needed to model the branches individually, and then rig them to slide and pivot where they met the trunk. When his head turns, for example, all the branches on his neck slide and rotate, much like a mechanical object. That made for some extremely complex riggingi The same philosophy applied to Groot's facial expressions. Again, we didn't want I1 / 27 the face to look elastic," said Aithadi, "so we decided that the lines on his face were ac-

GUARDIANS tually separations between plates of bark, and those plates moved as he made facial expressions. The only deformation was in his nose; everything else was sliding and shifting. We had to make some concessions, because we didn't want his movement to be so mechanical that he looked like a robot. So, we decided that the nose area between the eyes and the mouth could be a bit more loose. The lips could be looser, and the eyelids could be soft. Everything else we kept rigid." After animators had completed broad-stroke animation on Groot, the character was subjected to a procedural system that automatically added the mechanical effects, based on the position of the joints. "It was a really intricate system," related Aithadi, "and our rigging team did an amazing job with it. In fact, it was so intricate that we were asked to dial it back. In some cases, the movement was too complex. From our perspective, it was really cool; but the director saw that it took away from Groot's performance, so we had to simplify it a bit." To texture the character, MPC artists photographed many varieties of trees at hew Gardens in London. "In deciding on the textures," said Aithadi, "we had to figure out how old Groot would be - is he young, old, a teenager? We settled on an adolescent Groot, so it was important that we not make him look old as we were texturing him. That was quite difficult because wood is naturally gnarly and wrinkly; and so, it was a matter of finding the right type of wood, something that had the properties of wood, but wouldn't make him look old. In the end, Groot's textures were a mix of many different woods. ¿There was no one type of tree that worked completely as the basis for Groot. In fact, we 12 / 27 found that if we made him all of the same wood, he looked a bit boring and monochro-

matic. We had to be careful about too much variation, though, because that tended to make him look like a patchwork. It took a lot of experimentation to get just the right look." Groot's wood and bark surfaces were textured with a variety of mosses and lichen, as well, to add visual interest. set on the largest stage at Longcross - a stage second only to the 007 Stage at Shepperton in size - which allowed production to capture much of the prison action in camera. With previs as a guide to what parts of the prison would be seen from shot to shot, Framestore artists added 27 levels of prison to the practical set. "It was a very big build for us," said Jonathan Fawkner, "but building the prison was not the biggest challenge. We had a very good set scan, and we just needed to duplicate it. The bigger difficulty was lighting it. It was a very big space that only got bigger as it went up, because it was an inverted cone. What saved us was that the set had been decorated with robotic spotlights, called 'sharpies,' which moved around on a cycle. Those became our friends throughout the whole sequence because we could utilize them to strafe light across surfaces, which was much more interesting than just having these flat, repetitious prison levels. We used those lights to great effect. Additional lighting effects emanated from the head beams of CG hoverbots that engage the Guardians as they make their escape from the Kyln. "That wasn't part of the plan, originally," Fawkner recalled, "but I came up with the idea to flash the hoverbot beams into the camera lens, which added more interest to the shots. It was risky because it meant possibly having to add those lights to the set and characters in the plates, as well. We didn't really know until we'd done every shot whether or not it was going to work. But, in the end, we didn't have to do that too much. The sequence is frenetic enough that people don't notice where every light is hitting. I think having those hoverbot lights lifted the sequence and gave it a different look than it would have had otherwisei 14 / 27 As a Framestore sequence, the prison escape was one that had Framestore inte-

grating MPC's Groot character into its pipeline and shots. Framestore also did some additional Groot rigging for a scene in which the character grows a mass of twigs and branches as armor against guards shooting at him.iWe asked the question one day, 'What happens when Groot gets shot?'" recalled Fawkner. "There was a lot of scratching of heads as we tried to figure that out. Should he get bullet holes that then heal up? No, that's been done before. Finally, we came up with this concept of his growing an armor of twigs, vines and branches. Despite a slightly futuristic setting and alien combatants, Edge of Tomorrow - directed by Doug Liman and starring Tom Cruise - was more war movie than science fiction, and was peppered with images evoking archival D-Day combat footage.
